segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finally then, brothers and sisters, we ask you and urge you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, as indeed you are walking, you do so more and more.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is God's will, your holiness: that you abstain from sexual immorality;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that each of you know how to gain control over your own body in holiness and honor,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not in lustful passion, like the Gentiles who do not know God;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that no one overstep and take advantage of a brother or sister in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, just as we told you before and solemnly warned you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God did not call us for impurity but in holiness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, whoever rejects this is rejecting not a human being but God, who also gives his Holy Spirit to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now about love for your brothers and sisters, you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and indeed you do this toward all the brothers and sisters throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers and sisters, to do so more and more,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to make it your ambition to live quietly, to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, just as we instructed you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you may walk respectably before outsiders and have need of no one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers and sisters, about those who are asleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest, who have no hope.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if we believe that Jesus died and rose, so also God, through Jesus, will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this we say to you by a word of the Lord: we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will certainly not go ahead of those who have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Lord himself will come down from heaven with a shout of command, with an archangel's voice and with God's trumpet, and the dead in Christ will rise first;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will always be with the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, comfort one another with these words.

notes.note: The Greek masculine plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and the letter is written to the whole congregation. 'Brothers' alone now suggests only men, so the inclusive form is used here, as in several recent translations. In verse 6 the singular is likewise rendered 'a brother or sister', though the instruction there is framed from a male point of view.

notes.phrase: gain control over your own body
notes.note: The Greek says literally 'to acquire (or gain mastery of) his own vessel'. 'Vessel' is a metaphor, and interpreters have been divided since antiquity. One reading takes it as one's own body, perhaps specifically the sexual organ, giving 'control your own body'. The other takes it as a wife, giving 'take a wife for himself'. Both have serious scholarly support, since the verb more naturally means 'acquire', which favours 'wife', while 'his own' and the wider usage of 'vessel' favour 'body'. The text follows the reading most recent translations adopt.

The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples, and elsewhere in this translation the same word appears as 'nations' where peoples as such are meant. Paul's readers were themselves largely non-Jews, so here the word marks those outside the community, as the added phrase 'who do not know God' shows; that phrase echoes Old Testament language.

notes.traditional: in any matter / in this matter
notes.note: The Greek has 'in the matter', which most interpreters take as the sexual conduct just discussed: the wrong would be adultery, which defrauds a fellow believer. The word can also mean a business dealing, and some older translations and a minority of scholars read the verse as a new topic, dishonesty in commerce. The verb rendered 'take advantage of' often has a financial sense, which gives that minority view some support.

notes.phrase: love for your brothers and sisters
notes.note: In ordinary Greek this word meant the affection between actual siblings. Early Christian writers applied it to the bond between members of the community, who regarded one another as family. The rendering here is matched to 'brothers and sisters' elsewhere in the chapter. 'Taught by God' translates a single compound word that appears to have been coined by Paul.

The Greek form can be masculine ('no one') or neuter ('nothing'), so the phrase means either 'depend on no one' or 'lack nothing'. The context of working with one's own hands suits either, and translations are divided. The practical point is the same: believers should support themselves and not live off others.

Sleep was a common euphemism for death in both Greek and Jewish usage, and the readers would have understood at once that the dead are meant, as verse 16 says outright. The image is kept because Paul uses it three times here. By itself it does not settle what he believed about the state of the dead before the resurrection.

notes.traditional: them also which sleep in Jesus
notes.note: In the Greek, 'through Jesus' stands between 'those who have fallen asleep' and 'will bring', and it can attach to either. The text takes it with the verb, so that God brings them through Jesus. Many translations and commentators take it with the participle, giving 'those who have fallen asleep through Jesus', that is, who died as believers. The word order slightly favours that second reading, and the sense slightly favours the first; the question remains open.

notes.phrase: by a word of the Lord
notes.traditional: by the word of the Lord
notes.note: Paul claims the Lord's authority for what follows, but the phrase does not say how he received it. It may refer to a saying of Jesus handed down in tradition, whether one not preserved in the Gospels or a summary of teaching like Matthew 24:30-31. It may instead refer to a revelation given through a Christian prophet, possibly Paul himself. Scholars are divided.

The Greek word means both 'arrival' and 'presence'. In the period it was regularly used for the official visit of a king, emperor or high official to a city, an occasion marked by public ceremony. Readers in a city like Thessalonica would probably have heard that association when the word was applied to the Lord.

The verb means to seize or snatch away suddenly and by force. The Latin translation of this verse used the verb rapere, and the English word 'rapture' derives from it. The term and the later doctrinal systems built around it are not in the Greek text itself.

The noun translated 'to meet' was often used for a city's residents going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him back in. Many scholars think Paul draws on that custom, which would imply that the Lord's people accompany him as he arrives. Others hold that the word is too ordinary to carry this weight. Paul does not say here where the company goes next, only that they will always be with the Lord.

candidates.reason: The plural address and the singular 'brother' recur in nearly every letter, and translators split between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'believers'; readers would be confused by variation.
It recurs across the Gospels, Acts, the letters and Revelation with renderings ranging from 'fornication' to 'sexual immorality' to 'prostitution', and its scope is debated.

Translators alternate between 'sanctification', 'holiness' and 'consecration' across Romans, 1 Corinthians, the Thessalonian letters and Hebrews, and it should sit consistently alongside the ἅγιος entry.
The Semitic idiom for conduct is frequent in Paul and John, and translations vary between 'walk', 'live' and 'conduct yourselves'; one policy is needed on whether to keep the metaphor.
The verb and its noun παράκλησις span urge, encourage, comfort and appeal throughout the New Testament, and a sense-by-sense rule would keep chapters consistent.
